title: Boss: the deploy script review
summary: Finish a real log-rotation script: getopts, trap cleanup and a dry run, all checked by running it.

steps.title: Code review
body: Code review: the team's log-rotation script goes into cron next week. Finish its option parsing, make a teammate's
build script clean up after itself, and make the rotation itself work, with a dry run. Every check runs your script

steps.title: Parse options with getopts
prompt: `~/bin/rotate-logs` is a script the team will run from cron. Its options are not parsed yet. Using `getopts`, make it:
- accept `-n` (dry run) and `-k DAYS` (default `7`), then exactly **one** positional argument, `DIR`;
- print its settings exactly like `dir=/var/log/app keep=3 dry_run=1`;
- on an unknown option, a `-k` without a value, or a missing `DIR`: print a line containing `usage` to **stderr**
and exit with code `2` (the convention for "you called me wrong").

checks.name: an unknown option exits 2 with usage on stderr
checks.fail: `rotate-logs -z /x` should print a usage line on stderr and exit 2.

checks.name: -k without a value exits 2
checks.fail: `rotate-logs -k` (no value) should exit 2. A leading `:` in the optstring (`":nk:"`) lets you handle it yourself.

hints: `while getopts ":nk:" opt; do case $opt in n) dry_run=1 ;; k) keep=$OPTARG ;; *) usage ;; esac; done`. A colon after a letter means it takes a value.
After the loop, `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` drops the options, so `$1` is DIR. Then `[ $# -eq 1 ] || usage`.

`usage() { echo "usage: rotate-logs [-n] [-k DAYS] DIR" >&2; exit 2; }`. Note `/x -k`: getopts stops at the first non-option, so `-k` ends up as a second positional argument, which the `$# -eq 1` test rejects.
solution: usage() { echo "usage: rotate-logs [-n] [-k DAYS] DIR" >&2; exit 2; }
steps.explain: `getopts` is built into every POSIX shell and handles `-nk 3`, `-k3` and `--` for you. It only does short options; for `--long` ones, scripts either loop over `$@` with `case` or move to a real language. Exit code 2 for misuse is what `grep`, `ls` and most tools return, so callers can tell "you called me wrong" from "it failed".

steps.title: Clean up with trap, even on failure
prompt: Review comment on `~/bin/build-report`: *"Every failed run leaves a `/tmp/build-report.NNN` folder behind, and a fixed
name in `/tmp` is unsafe on a shared machine."* Try `~/bin/build-report /no/file ~/out.txt; ls -d /tmp/build-report.*`.
Fix it: create the scratch folder with `mktemp -d`, and remove it with a `trap ... EXIT`, so it goes away whether the
script succeeds, fails under `set -e`, or is interrupted. A good run must still write the counts to OUTPUT.

checks.name: a good run still works
checks.fail: `build-report ~/data/orders.txt ~/out.txt` should write the counts, `3 mug` first.

checks.name: a failed run leaves nothing in /tmp
checks.cmd: m=$(mktemp); sleep 0.1; ~/bin/build-report /no/such/file ~/out.txt >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?; left=$(find /tmp -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -newer "$m" ! -path "$m"); rm -f "$m"; echo "exit $rc, left behind: $left"; test "$rc" -ne 0 && test -z "$left"
checks.fail: A failed run must exit non-zero and leave nothing new in `/tmp`. `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT` runs on every exit, including the one `set -e` causes.

checks.name: a good run leaves nothing in /tmp
checks.fail: A successful run left something in `/tmp`.

checks.name: the scratch folder comes from mktemp
checks.fail: Create the folder with `work=$(mktemp -d)`: a random, private name instead of a guessable one.

hints: Right after it: `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT`. Then the last `rm -rf` line is no longer needed.
With sed: `sed -i 's#^work=.*#work=$(mktemp -d)#; s#^mkdir "$work"#trap '\''rm -rf "$work"'\'' EXIT#; /^rm -rf/d' ~/bin/build-report`, or rewrite the file with a here-doc.
solution: # build-report INPUT OUTPUT: counts how often each line of INPUT occurs, biggest first, into OUTPUT.
explain: `set -e` makes a script stop at the first failure, which is good, but every line after it is skipped, including
your cleanup. `trap ... EXIT` is the shell's `finally`. Note what `set -e` does **not** catch: a failing command in
an `if` condition, before `||` or `&&`, or inside `$(...)` that is part of another command. Check those by hand.

steps.title: Rotate logs for real
prompt: `~/bin/rotate-logs` now parses its options. Finish the job it describes in its `TODO`. In `DIR` only (not below it):
2. `gzip` the `.log` files **older than KEEP days** (`-k`, default 7);
3. with `-n`, **print** each command instead of running it (a line with `rm` and the file, or `gzip` and the file),
Test it on `~/logs/app` (`ls -l --time-style=+%F ~/logs/app` shows the ages). The checks run it on a fresh copy
of that folder, so your test runs do not matter.

checks.name: a dry run lists the work
checks.cmd: d=$(mktemp -d); cp -a /opt/dojo/state/applogs/. "$d"/; out=$(~/bin/rotate-logs -n "$d" 2>&1); echo "$out"; grep -E "gzip.*c\.log" <<<"$out" >/dev/null && grep -E "gzip.*d\.log" <<<"$out" >/dev/null && grep -E "rm.*f\.log\.gz" <<<"$out" >/dev/null && ! grep -E "(gzip|rm).*(a\.log|b\.log|e\.log\.gz|notes)" <<<"$out" >/dev/null
checks.fail: With `-n` it should print a `gzip` line for `c.log` and `d.log` and an `rm` line for `f.log.gz`, and nothing for the other files.

checks.name: a dry run changes nothing
checks.fail: The dry run changed files. With `-n`, only print.

checks.name: a real run rotates
checks.cmd: d=$(mktemp -d); cp -a /opt/dojo/state/applogs/. "$d"/; ~/bin/rotate-logs "$d" >/dev/null 2>&1; ls "$d" | tr "\n" " "; test "$(ls "$d" | tr "\n" " ")" = "a.log b.log c.log.gz d.log.gz e.log.gz notes.txt "
checks.fail: After a real run the folder should hold `a.log b.log c.log.gz d.log.gz e.log.gz notes.txt` (shown first). Delete old `.gz` before compressing: `gzip` keeps the old file's date, so a fresh `d.log.gz` is "40 days old" too.

checks.name: -k changes the age
checks.fail: With `-k 2`, `b.log` (3 days old) should be compressed and `a.log` (1 day) kept.

hints: `find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.log' -mtime +"$keep"` lists what to compress. `-maxdepth 1` keeps it out of subfolders; `-mtime +7` means more than 7 whole days.
A tiny helper keeps dry runs honest: `run() { if [ "$dry_run" = 1 ]; then echo "$*"; else "$@"; fi; }`, then `run gzip -- "$f"`.
Loop safely over the names: `find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do run rm -- "$f"; done`, then the same for `.log` with `gzip`.
solution: run() { if [ "$dry_run" = 1 ]; then echo "$*"; else "$@"; fi; }
find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do run rm -- "$f"; done
find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.log' -mtime +"$keep" -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do run gzip -- "$f"; done
explain: On most servers `logrotate` does this job (with `compress`, `maxage`, `copytruncate` or a `postrotate` reload), and
`journald` rotates its own files. Scripts like this one still exist for app folders logrotate does not know about. The
habits that make them safe are the ones you used: a dry-run flag, NUL-separated names, `--` before file names,
strict mode and a clean exit code.
